title: Methodology
text:
Game state. The scoreline from a team’s point of view at the moment of an event: winning, drawing or losing. Minutes in each state are measured from the minutes goals were scored. Match length is taken as the later of 97 minutes and the last recorded event.
Supremacy. The expected goal difference (home minus away) implied by Pinnacle’s pre-match Asian handicap and goal lines. Expected goals and supremacy are solved together from the two lines with a root-finder. Team supremacy is that value from the team’s own side (flipped for away teams).
Repeater. A corner by the same team, in the same half, within one minute of that team’s previous corner. Repeaters are given a value of 0.
Adjusted corner value. For a corner won by side s (home/away) in state g at team supremacy x:

\text{value} = \frac{\bar r_s}{\alpha_{s,g} + \beta_{s,g}\,x}

where \bar r_s is the league’s average corner rate for side s, and (\alpha, \beta) come from a line fitted to corners-per-minute across 30 supremacy buckets for that league, side and state. In the full model the fit is weighted by minutes in each bucket, and closed-doors COVID matches are excluded from fitting.

title: Methodology
text:
Ratings and prediction

Each team has an attack rating (corners won) and a defence rating (corners conceded): rolling means over its last N matches (12, 15, 19, 25 or 30), using only matches played before the fixture being predicted.
Four metrics are compared: raw counts, raw without repeaters (nr), adjusted values (adj), and adjusted without repeaters (adj_nr).
Home corners are predicted with OLS on the home attack rating, the away defence rating and match supremacy. Away corners are predicted the same way, the other way round.
Promoted and relegated teams keep their ratings across divisions. Supremacy in the new league’s fixtures accounts for the change in opposition.

title: Methodology
text:
Betting backtest

Test period: 2024/25 and 2025/26. The OLS model is fitted only on earlier seasons, and predictions are rescaled to the test period’s league corner level.
Market: Pinnacle Asian corner handicap. Its implied corner supremacy is compared with the model’s predicted home-minus-away corners.
Selection: a 1-unit bet on the side the model prefers when the two differ by 0.5 corners or more (a threshold sweep is shown in the analysis).
Settlement: actual raw corners at Pinnacle’s quoted odds, including quarter-line half-win and half-loss handling and pushes on whole lines.
Totals: corner over/under was backtested with the same set-up and lost money in every configuration. It’s no longer part of the live model.

title: Methodology
text:
Code
The processing code for the original study is in the code/ folder of this site’s repository. The small data snapshots behind every chart and table are in snapshots/.

title: A Game State Adjusted Corner Model
text:
Corner betting markets rate teams on how many corners they win and concede. But the number of corners a team gets in any given match depends a lot on the scoreline and on how strong the opponent is, and over a short run of fixtures those two things skew the raw counts. This project removes that bias by valuing every corner in the context it was won and builds team ratings from the adjusted values.



45 leagues modelled


139,172 matches


1.4m corner events valued


4.1% ROI on corner handicap markets


Summary

Game state has a large effect on corners. Across the 45 leagues modelled the median league, the home side’s share of corners is 16 points higher when losing than when winning.
Over short time periods, teams can spend disproportionate amounts of time in winning or losing positions, so raw corner counts become skewed by game state effects.
Valuing each corner by its game state, its home/away context, the pre-match supremacy, and dropping “repeater” corners, gives ratings that predict future corners better than raw counts do at every window length tested.
Against real Pinnacle prices, the adjusted ratings are profitable in the corner handicap market across all 8 rating sets tested. The best rating set had an ROI of 4.1% across 3,486 bets during the testing window. They show no edge in predicting corner totals.
The optimal ratings framework derived from this testing now powers an active betting model. An automated workflow scrapes upcoming fixtures, derives current team ratings, makes predictions and compares this to the current Pinnacle prices. These predictions are sent to a dashboard that shows me recommended bets each day.

2. The data
Two scrapers feed the model. Each runs automatically every day through a cloud based automated workflow. The raw output is archived, and the processing stages read from there.

totalcorner.com: match events
The first scraper collects every finished match in 45 leagues from totalcorner.com. Each match has:

an event timeline: every goal, corner and card, with the minute it happened
full-time match stats: corners, shots on and off target, attacks, dangerous attacks and possession for each side
pre-match betting lines shown on the match page: the Asian handicap, goal line and corner line, with their odds

Results are stored in a local database and exported as one CSV per league. The same scraper also collects upcoming fixtures for the live model.

How it’s used. The timeline gives the scoreline at every minute of every match. From this we can work out how long each team spent winning, drawing and losing, and which game state each corner was won in. The pre-match handicap and goal lines are converted into each match’s expected goals and supremacy, a market-implied measure of the relative strength of each team.


Odds to expected goals and supremacy → code/odds_to_goals.py


Why it’s useful. Most data sources only contain team and match totals. That can’t tell you whether a team’s corners came while chasing a game or while protecting a lead. The minute-by-minute timeline is what makes the game-state adjustments possible, and its coverage of second-tier leagues means promoted and relegated teams can be tracked across divisions.


Pinnacle: corner market prices
Another scraper pulls Pinnacle prices once a day for every fixture in the next seven days.This includes Asian handicap lines, goal lines, as well as corner handicap and corner totals. A processing step removes Pinnacle’s margin and fits a Poisson distribution (totals) and a Skellam distribution (handicap) to find the implied corner total and supremacy.
The archive covers 21,798 matches scraped since August 2022.

How it’s used. Pinnacle’s corner supremacy is the benchmark the model has to beat. In the backtest, the model’s predicted supremacy is compared with Pinnacle’s for each match. When the two disagree by a specific threshold, a one unit bet is placed at Pinnacle’s quoted odds and settled on the actual outcome. In the live model, the same comparison flags value bets on upcoming fixtures.
Why it’s useful. Pinnacle is widely regarded as the sharpest bookmaker - it runs low margins and doesn’t restrict winning customers, so its prices are the best estimate of the “true” market view. Generally, a model that beats Pinnacle has found a real edge rather than just a soft bookmaker. It is also the only bookmaker I have an active account with so if I want to build a model that can be profitable in real time it will need to beat Pinnacle lines.

The raw event data goes through three processing steps before any analysis: working out the game state at every event, adding up the minutes and corners each team had in each state, and flagging repeater corners.

Identifying game state at each match event

Identifying repeaters
A repeater is a corner that comes straight after another corner by the same team. Repeaters are not statistically independent events: they depend on the corner before them. A team can pick up two or more corners in quick succession, but this is not a fair reflection of their corner-generating strength. Over a small sample of games, a few of these spells can skew a team’s ratings.
Our minute-level event data allows us to identify repeaters. A corner is flagged as a repeater if the previous event was also a corner, taken by the same team, in the same half, and no more than one minute earlier.

title: A Game State Adjusted Corner Model
text:
4. Analysis

Game state affects corner rates
Teams that are behind attack more, so they win more corners. Teams that are ahead tend to sit deeper and win fewer. The chart shows the home side’s share of all corners in each league, split by the game state at the time.


Home share of corners (%) by scoreline


                            
                                            


The size of the effect varies a lot by league: from about 4 points in Scotland Premiership to 26 points in Spain Segunda. Tactical cultures, the prevalence of away fans and the role of dominant teams in each league all play a part in explaining these disparities. Any adjustment has to be league-specific.


Short runs of games can distort raw corner counts
If every team’s game state minutes were proportionate to their underlying strength, game state biases woul be less prevalent in the raw counts. However, football matches are messy and chaotic, and over short samples of games teams spend disproportionate amounts of time in game states that do not reflect their underlying strength.
The left panel shows how long each Premier League side should have spent winning, drawing and losing over the first nine games of 2023/24, based on the pre-match lines. The right panel shows how long they actually did.


                            
                                            


Several teams spent far more or far less time losing than their strength implied. Their raw corner numbers could be inflated or deflated as a result.


Supremacy matters in every game state
Stronger teams win more corners, and that holds whether they’re winning, drawing or losing. To measure it, each league’s team-matches are split into 30 equal-sized buckets by pre-match supremacy, separately for home and away sides. Within each bucket I calculate corners per minute in each game state, then fit a line per state, weighted by the minutes behind each bucket.
Pick a league:


Corners per minute vs pre-match supremacy


                            
                                            


Each dot is one supremacy bucket, and hovering shows how many minutes are in that bucket. Across all leagues, losing sides win corners fastest and winning sides slowest, and the lines rise with supremacy. Together, the six lines give an expected corner rate for any combination of home/away, game state and supremacy, which drives the adjusted corner values later in this section.


Supremacy buckets and fitted lines → code/adjusted_values.py




Repeaters are stable across teams
Each dot below is one team, showing the share of its corners that were repeaters (defined in section 3):


Repeater rate by team (teams with 100+ matches)


                            
                                            


The rate is stable at around 13–15% across leagues and across teams within each league: 90% of the 310 teams fall between 11% and 16%. So removing repeaters doesn’t penalise any particular style of play. It just removes correlated noise.


Adjusted corner values
Each corner is valued as the average corner rate divided by the rate we’d expect given the context it was won in:

\text{value} = \frac{\text{average rate}_{\text{home/away}}}{\text{expected rate}(\text{home/away},\ \text{game state},\ \text{supremacy})}

A corner won where corners are usually rare (a big underdog, while winning) is worth more than 1. One won where they’re usually plentiful (a big favourite chasing the game) is worth less than 1. Repeaters are worth 0.
Case study: Rayo Vallecano 1–2 Barcelona, 27 August 2024. Barcelona went in as 0.77-goal favourites. Rayo scored in the 9th minute, Barcelona equalised in the 60th and won it with an 82nd-minute goal.

Drawing: Rayo corners are worth 1.35 and Barcelona’s 0.81. The gap reflects the difference in team strength alone.
Rayo winning: a Rayo corner is worth 1.96, because an underdog protecting a lead rarely wins corners. Barcelona’s are worth 0.62, because a favourite chasing the game typically wins more corners.

Once you account for the relative strength of the teams and the game state effect - Barcelona chasing the game for more than 50 minutes, Rayo’s corner performance looks more impressive than Barcelona’s, even with two of their repeater corners removed.


Buckets, fitted lines and adjusted values → code/adjusted_values.py


Because supremacy is stripped out of each corner’s value, a team’s rating no longer depends as much on who it has played. That means shorter rating windows can be used, so changes of manager or personnel show up sooner. It also means promoted and relegated teams carry their ratings between divisions without special handling. The prediction model then adds supremacy back in as a separate input, taken from the upcoming match’s betting lines.

title: A Game State Adjusted Corner Model
section: 5. Building and testing a predictive model
text:
5. Building and testing a predictive model

Building adjusted corner ratings
Team attack and defence ratings are built as rolling averages over the last N games, divided by the average for the league over the same period to give a ratio. The average ratio for the league is 1.00.
Four metrics were tested:

raw: raw corner counts
nr: raw counts with repeaters removed
adj: adjusted corner values
adj_nr: adjusted corner values with repeaters removed

The table shows current ratings for every Premier League team on each metric. Higher attack means a team wins more corners, and higher defence means it concedes more. Use the buttons to switch metric, and click a column to sort.



  
    rawnradjadj_nr
  
  



Team
Home attack
Home defence
Away attack
Away defence






  




On raw counts, Man City, Chelsea and Liverpool have the highest home attack ratings. However on the adj metric Bournemouth, Newcastle and Leeds top the list. This shows much of the big clubs’ raw advantage comes from being favourites and the adjustment strips that out.
Ratings use a 19-game window, the same as the live model, and are as of 12 September 2026.


Adjusted ratings make better predictions
Each set of ratings, together with match supremacy, feeds an OLS model that predicts each side’s corners for matches in the test dataset. The chart shows the R² improvement over raw counts, for each window length.


Out-of-sample R², % change vs raw corner ratings


                            
                                            


The adjusted metrics beat raw counts at every window length on both sides. The gain is largest for home corners, which are the most sensitive to game state. Removing repeaters from raw counts (nr) makes little difference on its own by this metric; almost all of the gain comes from the game-state and supremacy adjustment.






R² values of around 0.1 are normal here. Match-level corner counts are dominated by Poisson-like randomness, so no pre-match model explains most of the variance. What matters for betting is whether the model beats the market, which is tested next.





Beating the market
The model’s predicted corner supremacy is compared with Pinnacle’s implied corner supremacy for every priced match in 2024/25 and 2025/26. The prediction model is fitted only on earlier seasons, and ratings use only matches played before each fixture. When the two differ by 0.5 corners or more, a 1-unit bet goes on the side the model prefers, at Pinnacle’s price. Every bet is settled on actual corner outcomes.

All 8 adjusted rating sets are profitable in the handicap market, at between 2.1–4.1% ROI.


How the edge scales
Raising the minimum threshold before betting shows the balance between ROI and volume. We are interested in finding the threshold that maximises units won.


                            
                                            


Betting every match loses money. Once the model disagrees by 0.20 corners or more, ROI becomes positive. It peaks at 143 units at a 0.50-corner threshold. ROI rises as the threshold increases, however overall units won falls as fewer bets are being placed. Above 1.2 corners the ROI projections get noisy, because there are much fewer bets.
The totals market is different. The same ratings were backtested against Pinnacle’s corner over/under lines, and every metric/window combination lost money. My working hypothesis is that game state shifts which side wins the corners much more than it changes how many corners there are in total, so correcting for it helps the handicap market and doesn’t help totals.
